## Abstract

In the US, birth defects result in over 139,000 hospitalizations, costing $2.6B and leaving the

patient with lifelong treatments, disabilities, illness, or even death which can largely impact the

individual and their family’s life. MRI anthropomorphic phantoms can accelerate and enhance

the development of sequences and image processing algorithms, improving diagnostic and

treatment efficacies. Our lab has evaluated the existing fetal MRI phantoms, revealing that 7%

include physiological motion. In response to this, we have developed a 6 DOF robot to integrate

physiological motion for a fetal phantom used in the gravid abdomen. This robot has been

tested to have a positioning accuracy of ±2.1 mm (SD 0.87 mm) and orientation accuracy of

±1.7° (SD 2.9°). After acquiring MR images, the robot has been shown to degrade image SNR

less than 2% with a maximum B0 variation of 1 ppm supporting its MR compatibility and minimal

impact on images.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

Birth defects most commonly start developing in the first three months of pregnancy. These can

require infrequent or lifelong treatments, disabilities, illness, or even death which can largely

impact the individual and their family’s life. When large numbers of people experience these

issues, there is a significant burden on health care systems and societies. An estimated 6% or

7.9 million annual births globally experience serious birth defects which are the leading cause of

infant mortality and are responsible for 1 in 5 infant deaths [1]. Over 3.3 million children less

than 5 years of age die each year from birth defects, with millions being mentally or physically

disabled [1]. This issue has been largely overlooked as it has been estimated that about 70% of

birth defects could be prevented, repaired or ameliorated [1]. In the United States of America

(USA), each year birth defects or congenital anomalies affect 1 of 33 babies born [2]. As of

2004, this accounted for over 139,000 hospitalizations, costing $2.6 billion [3]. Between 1997

and 2004, hospitalization rates increased by 28.5 percent for cardiac and circulatory congenital

anomalies and 25.3 percent for digestive congenital anomalies (when noted as either the

principal or a coexisting condition) [3]. More recently, 19,578 infant deaths were recorded for

2020 in the USA with a rate of 5.42 infant deaths per 1,000 live births [4]. Additionally, neonatal

and post-natal mortality rates were 3.56 and 1.86. The five leading causes of infant deaths were

congenital malformations (21%), disorders related to short gestation and low birth weight (16%),

sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) (7%), unintentional injuries (6%), and maternal

complications (6%). Appendix A: Stats for Common Birth Defects, Tables A1-A3 showcase the

volumes and hospital implications associated with some common birth defects. In Canada,

these numbers are higher at 1 in 25 babies born with birth defects and account for 28% of infant

deaths as of 2012 [5]. Moreover, an estimated 29% of taxpayers’ money was estimated to be

spent on our $264.4 billion health care costs in 2019 [6].

Pregnant mothers routinely have ultrasound (US) imaging appointments to monitor the health of

their baby and themselves. It is advantageous to use US for screening due to its lower cost,

operator and patient comfort/convenience, wider availability, and real time results. Due to the

images being low resolution, it can be difficult to draw conclusions if symptoms of anomalies are

present. This is particularly a problem when observing small scale structures in the developing

fetal brain, among other regions. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used as a follow up

method to acquire more information since it is the only other imaging modality that can safely

image the fetus without the use of ionizing radiation. Other advantages include its high

resolution, excellent soft tissue contrast, and its flexibility to acquire a variety of different types of

images. For these reasons, MRI usage in fetal imaging has been increasing and has been

shown to improve diagnostic accuracy while preventing misdiagnosis [7], [8]. Between 1996 and

2016, the rate of pregnancies exposed to MRI has increased from 1.0 to 11.9 per 1000 USA

pregnancies and 0.5 to 9.8 per 1000 Ontarian pregnancies [9]. However, many of the fetal

structures that need to be observed are very small and move around quickly. When an image is

taken slowly compared to the motion of an object in the frame, the acquired images are

distorted and blurry. This makes it challenging to acquire large amounts of information in short

amounts of time.

While scanning, image quality is often degraded from sources of motion including maternal

respiration and bowel movement as well as fetal gross body, respiration and cardiac movement.

The presence of motion artifacts in images necessitates several rescans and localizations of the

patient to obtain sufficient information. Small scale structures can no longer be detected

accurately, and tissue boundaries become difficult to delineate from blurring. These issues stem

from the use of accelerated adult sequences to reduce the motion artifacts, but the images are

acquired with lower resolution as a compromise and continue to be frequently distorted. Several

studies have reported excluding 40-80% of acquired images due to excessive motion artifacts in

addition to attempting 2-3 scans to obtain satisfactory images [10]-[15].

Many methods have been attempted to reduce motion including the use of maternal sedation.

However, even if the fetus remains still, motion may still occur from maternal respiration or

bowel movements [16]. Other methods have been reported like change of diet, breath holding

with respiratory gating, scanning during early mornings, emptying of the bowel, laying the

patient in certain positions, increasing the field of view to keep the regions of interest in the

frames and decreasing the field of view to decrease slice acquisition times. Even while

employing all of these methods independently or selectively, motion artifacts remain the largest

problem. Voluntary maternal motion can usually be attributed to discomfort, lack of

communication with the imaging team, or stress. Few studies have used animal testing which

continues to be costly and time consuming, with its own limitations such as the need for animal

sedation. It is generally not accurate or comparable to human imaging [17].

Research towards minimizing the manifestation of motion artifacts in images has taken two

main approaches: sequence optimization and image processing. Sequence optimization is a

preventative approach where experimentation can reveal how to tune sequences for specific

applications, making better use of the hardware. Alternatively, machine learning based image

processing algorithms can be used to correct motion distortion for enhanced image quality.

Volunteers for both sequence optimization and image processing algorithms take extensive

amounts of time to recruit with compensation for patients often provided [16]. The data

collection process is very slow, requiring some hospitals and labs to have dedicated teams to

recruit patients, only increasing costs. In the development of image processing algorithms,

datasets are largely limited in quality and size; there are no motion free reference images or

images with known motion to base these algorithms on [19]. It is common for researchers to

manually edit images and add synthetic distortions simulating motion [20]-[23]. Further, with

irreproducible motion it is difficult to build accurate algorithms. In each of these approaches,

there is a lack of formal experimentation which is key for achieving repeatable results.

Imaging phantoms can be used to replace the need for volunteers, but need to mimic the

anatomy, relaxation/dielectric properties, and motion of the target tissue. Our lab has reviewed

the existing fetal MRI phantoms showing an average overall accuracy of 26%, with merely 7%

of phantoms also including physiological motion [18]. To the best of our knowledge, there have

been no new relevant papers on anthropomorphic MRI phantom of the fetal gross body that

have been published since our literature review. This review evaluated 17 phantoms that can be

broken down into anatomical categories as follows: 5 fetal gross body/gravid uterus, 1 brain, 2

lung, 1 fetal body tissue, 3 heart, 4 blood vessel, and 1 placenta phantom. None of the

phantoms included gross body motion, and 6 of the cardiovascular (heart & blood vessel)

phantoms included some sort of motion in the form of heart contractions or flow. The most

accurate phantom scored 9 out of 12 points, also being the most comprehensive by including

the uterus, fetus brain, fetus body (no limbs), eyeballs and placenta [24]. Each of the materials

reproduced the relaxometry and conductivity values of the respective tissues using agar-based

gels. There are, however, two large limitations in this solution. Since agar-based materials were

used, they had to be cast into 3D printed shells which affect the delineation of the tissue

boundaries and introduce artifacts due to the embedded plastic shells. Secondly, despite

satisfying all the criteria for anatomy and tissue mimicking aspects, no sources of motion were

incorporated and, hence, it cannot be used as a motion phantom. In contrast, the highest

scoring phantom in the motion category was a 3D printed biventricular heart valve [25], awarded

1 out of 3 points for including cardiovascular motion, but neglecting gross body motion. This

phantom simulated cardiac contraction and flow but was not composed of tissue mimicking

materials.

In conclusion, the current lack of effective phantoms capable of simulating gross body motion

poses a significant challenge when it comes to testing motion correction approaches or motion

resistant sequences. Furthermore, certain sequences can induce tissue heating, making it

crucial to accurately select MR gradients for fetal safety. Therefore, developing realistic motion

simulation techniques would greatly enhance our ability to address these concerns and improve

overall magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) outcomes.

This thesis aims to overcome these barriers by developing a novel anthropomorphic MRI motion

phantom of the gravid abdomen. The specific objectives are to (1) design and build a six

degrees of freedom (DOF) robot, (2) assess the MR compatibility of the robot, and (3) evaluate

the motion accuracy of the robot. The resulting fetal motion phantom allows users to prescribe

motion patterns that mimic physiological conditions, facilitating the advancement of MR

sequences and image processing algorithms. Ultimately, the resulting motion phantom promises

to enhance the diagnostic capabilities of MRI for fetal applications.

### 1.2 Contributions

The thesis makes significant contributions to the field of fetal anthropomorphic MRI phantoms,

including the following innovations:

1. Development of a device enabling gross body motion with a fetal anthropomorphic MRI

phantom in six degrees of freedom (6 DOF).

2. Achievement of a remarkable positioning accuracy of 1 mm, ensuring precise and

realistic motion simulation.

3. Successful demonstration of the device's compatibility with magnetic resonance imaging

(MRI), ensuring accurate and reliable imaging results.

These contributions collectively advance the state-of-the-art in fetal MRI phantom development

and provide valuable tools for improving imaging techniques and protocols in the field.

### 1.4 Background

### 1.4.1 Fetal Movements

As the fetus develops, it exhibits relatively erratic behaviour through the movement of the limbs,

head and body of the fetus through twisting, extending and wiggling. Mouth movements,

breathing, eye movements, twitches and startles can further be observed less frequently [16]. It

is very difficult to quantify information such as the angle of the joints, range of motion, force

exerted and speed of contraction. Fetal gross body motion (especially the limbs) decreases with

gestational age due to the restricted space and mostly developed muscles although head

movement can still occur. The frequency of such movements is expected to be 14.8 minutes per

10 movements and mostly lasting under 3 seconds in a third trimester fetus [26], [27]. It has

further been observed for the fetal head to undergo a maximum translation and rotation and

speed of 55 mm and 60° respectively at speeds up to 30 mm/s [30]-[32], although it is more

common for movements to be 2.8-15.5 mm at 2.5-20 mm/s [32]. Important to note, the

displacement and speed values measured in these studies only account for the start and end

position, disregarding the path taken and potentially increasing the speed required.

Although a prenatal fetus cannot breathe due to its fluid filled lungs, it still experiences some

respiratory-like movements. The average fetal respiratory rate at 28-39 weeks of gestation is 43

breaths/min, creating a maximum displacement of 3-8 mm in the abdomen [33], [34].

### 1.4.2 Maternal Movements

The womb is a lively area with many sources of interference from maternal activity. With the

gastrointestinal (GI) tract in the neighbouring area, vibrations from peristalsis generate a series

of 2 to 3 waves of contractions simultaneously [35]. These waves exist in different regions of the

tract with about 3 waves occurring per minute and lasting 9 seconds in length [35]. Concurrent

with the peristalsis, there are also segmentation contractions which occur once per 3 minutes.

However, the magnitude of the effect on the uterus could not be determined through existing

literature.

Another source of motion artifacts is through maternal respiration which is caused from the

diaphragm pushing downwards on the uterus [33], [34]. The median breathing rate for 36-week

pregnant women was found to be 17 breaths per minute which is comparable to that of a non-

pregnant woman [36]. A separate study with varying ages from 25-35 weeks gestational age

determined the maximum displacement of a fetal heart from maternal respiration motion was

between 0.5 to 2.3 mm, with a median of 1.8 mm [37].

### 1.5  Relevant MRI Topics

### 1.5.1 Motion Artifacts

Whereas photography has data acquisition occur in image space, MRI acquires data in k-space

which is a representation of spatial frequencies. A very high level of the MR image production

pipeline is shown in Figure 1.1) MR image production process. K-space and the image are

related by the Fourier Transform (FT) with the samples in k-space describing the contribution of

a frequency to the entire image, hence, any discrepancy in k space can affect every pixel in the

resulting image [16]. When a larger group of pixels experiences a change, the center of k-space

is primarily affected. This is an important concept when planning k-space trajectories; the

patterns the data is sampled to fill k-space.


<!-- Page 20 -->


7

*Figure 1.1) MR image production process. Adapted from Ch9 – Spatial Characteristics of the MRI, Sprawls, open access.*

On the MRI side, there are several gradients used to acquire the desired information. Frequency

encoding samples all the rows in the matrix in a single echo whereas phase encoding collects

the k-space lines. Since frequency encoding lasts on the order of milliseconds, there is no

chance for motion to distort the information to produce artifacts. In comparison, phase encoding

lasts for seconds to minutes because it occurs in many steps. The speed of the motions is fast

enough to affect the phase encoding process, consequently artifacts within images will be

displayed in the phase encoding direction, regardless of the actual direction of motion [38], [39].

Motion artifacts manifest images in a variety of ways depending on the motion sources. Blurring

of sharp outlines and ghosting from periodic movements are both related to the signal

readout/frequency encoding process [16]. Additionally, signal voids or contrast changes may

occur with very fast patient motion. Signal loss from spin dephasing and the appearance of

undesired strong signals on the other hand, are related to the pulse sequence. Readout artifacts

usually arise from inconsistencies between the k-space data and the assumptions of the signal

model used in reconstruction [16]. The imaged object must remain stationary during the k-space

sampling when an inverse fast FT is used, otherwise artifacts will be present. Using these

principles, a number of characteristics can be observed: the most important parameter for the

appearance of artifacts is motion as a function of k-space position; sequential k-space trajectory

is fairly insensitive to motion that is slow and continuous; the location of motion in k-space is


<!-- Page 21 -->


8

significant since data corruption near the center of k-space produces stronger artifacts than the

periphery; persistent modulation in k-space intensifies artifacts.

Ghosting occurs when the periodic motion is synchronized with the acquisition of k-space while

blurring arises when the motion is random [39]. The number of clones depends on the

frequency that k-space is modulated, for example, if every second line is altered there will be

two clones. Partial clones may form if the periodic motion is slightly out of phase with the k-

space acquisition. Apart from the movement of solid structures, the flow of fluids can also

present image artifacts. Similar to how ghosts are produced from periodic motion, fluid flow can

often be decomposed into several sinusoids, producing ghosts [41].

Data inconsistencies resulting from motion produces artifacts in two ways: within slices and

between slices. When motion takes place throughout radiofrequency (RF) pulse excitations and

echo formations, the phase incoherence of moving spins at the echo time causes artifacts within

slices [38]. Signal is lost due to dephasing or spatial misregistration. In contrast, motion between

the acquisition of sequential phase encoding steps generates phase errors originating from

location and signal intensity discrepancies of the moving spins during phase encoding [40], [41],

[42]. MRI generates gradients and assumes tissues are stationary throughout the acquisition

process. Subtle movements can introduce incorrect phase accumulations, for example, spins

moving in the direction of the gradient are given additional phase, producing inconsistencies

[16]. The excitation history effect is when motion occurs between RF pulses used for excitation,

saturation or refocusing. Instead of applying all 3 pulses in the same area, motion changes

where each RF pulse is applied, reducing the desired spin evolution in combination with

producing undesired signals. The result is a possibility for a lower SNR, ghosting, signal

disturbances, or signal voids [16]. Another way disturbances arise is by affecting the magnetic

fields. The B0 field is a gradient, hence, movement changes the experienced field strength and

introduces magnetic susceptibility effects to the surrounding areas. Movement also disturbs the

B1 field and surface coils, leading to further discrepancies [16].

### 1.5.2 Artifacts and Compatibility

1.5.2.1 Magnetic Susceptibility

The magnetic susceptibility (χ) of a material is a unitless parameter that measures how much a

material is magnetized under a magnetic field. Three categories of magnetic materials exist


<!-- Page 22 -->


9

based on how they interact with a magnetic field: diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic.

Diamagnetic materials have paired valence electrons and so there is no permanent magnetic

moment on the atom [42]. These materials oppose the magnetic field and have weak

interactions, hence, they can be identified by χ<0. Both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic

materials have unpaired valence electrons that align with an applied magnetic field to

strengthen it [42]. These effects are far more pronounced in ferromagnetic materials as the

electrons are parallel, holding a lower energy state and becoming permanent magnets even

when the field is removed. While paramagnetic materials have χ>0, ferromagnetic materials

have χ>>0. A great image showing the different interactions between the magnetic materials

and field is shown in [42].

MRI acquisition is largely affected by the magnetic susceptibility of the imaged materials, but

artifacts arise mainly when there are sudden differences in the imaged region. Although there

are a number of different mechanisms by which errors can arise, a few particularly relevant

ones will be described in the next section.

1.5.2.2 Metals

Metals are widely used as structural components due to their strong mechanical properties. In

robotics applications, these largely help with positioning accuracy by supporting heavy loads

with minimal deformation. Also relevant, metals are used in the electronics to control the robot

such as wiring and motors. However, in an MRI environment, image quality and safety must be

preserved, which metals do not permit due to their interaction with the magnetic fields. A

number of concerns arise such as projectile hazards, heating and the introduction of image

artifacts. Artifacts can manifest images as include signal loss, high peripheral signal and

geometric distortions and the magnitude can depend on the metal composition, the interfacing

materials, and the imaging parameters [43].

Metals distort the static magnetic field of the MR scanner and introduce artifacts at interfaces

between tissues with different magnetic susceptibilities. The effects on the field typically depend

on the size and shape of the metal object along with the orientation of the magnetic field [43].

The altered precession frequencies of the protons and dephasing cause miss mapping of spatial

information, appearing black in images [41]. Frequency changes in both the slice selection and

readout directions displace the signal, interfering with their localization. For example, the slice

select gradient maps the frequencies to their respective positions. With variations in the static


<!-- Page 23 -->


10

magnetic field, the intended slice position is no longer an accurate representation of what is

actually selected. These effects are the same for the frequency encoding gradients.

Accordingly, signals can be shifted away from their intended region causing signal loss or they

can gather in another region forming a pile up artifact [43], [41]. With minor occurrences,

geometric distortions can be produced. Another consideration when dealing with metals is the

usage of fat suppression techniques. Most of these techniques are more sensitive to

fluctuations in the magnetic field resulting in failure of fat saturation near the metallic object.

1.5.2.3 MRI Compatible Materials

Maintaining the homogeneity of the magnetic field is a priority when imaging patients for

diagnostics, hence, the distortion a material introduces is an important design consideration.

Material selection affects many characteristics including the imaging (magnetic and electric) and

mechanical properties of the robot and so neither can be compromised. Several reviews have

been conducted to quantify the impact of various materials on the magnetic field and resulting

images [46], [47]. Although they are inconsistent in their methods, their findings have shown

relative trends and can be used to select materials appropriately. Generally, materials should

have as little interaction with the magnetic field as possible and should not experience any eddy

currents or electrical conductivity from RF pulses.

resonance frequency approaches the size of the imaged objects. High dielectric constants can

further attenuate the RF waves to induce variations in the B1 field [40]. As a result, flip angles

Another common practice to maintain a safe working environment is the use of MRI zones as

the public with no supervision and has a field strength of less than 0.5 mT. Zone 2 requires

supervision and is where the screening process takes place. Zone 3 is where the magnetic

fields are sufficiently strong to pose a hazard. Zone 4 is the MR magnet room itself. Most

magnet rooms are also marked on the floor where the field strength is 0.5 mT. This is accepted

as the projectile line where no potentially magnetic objects may enter due to the possibility of

becoming a projectile. Although many objects may not become a safety hazard at this point,

### 2.1.2 Robot Configurations

Most motion phantoms have 1-2 DOF because the anatomy they replicate is constrained by

surrounding tissues or muscles. Our fetal anthropomorphic motion phantom requires 6 DOF to

translate and/or rotate the fetus in any direction since it involves the entire body. In this

assembly, the motion created moves the entire fetus. The limbs are unable to function

independently as they would in a natural environment. This is due to the inability for the silicone

to have such a dynamic range of motion (ROM) and would require physical joints with actuators

to move each component. Since the boundaries of the different internal structures are the

regions of interest, the limbs are not substantially important. It is therefore sufficient to have the

limbs follow the body as it is moved, preventing the need for complex joints and actuation

methods integrated in the limbs. The most important parameter is the accuracy of the robot, with

other significant parameters being the workspace, speed, and the ability to distance actuators

from the phantom.

2.1.2.1 Serial Manipulators

The approach taken to design the robot is heavily influenced by its usage in the MRI. One

consideration is that positioning accuracy is vital which is somewhat challenging being unable to

use metals. Serial manipulators are known for their large workspaces they can reach in an open

loop chain. However, due to the sequential arrangement of the linkages and actuators, there is

an accumulation of error with each joint. This also makes it difficult to position the robot in the

MRI unless a horizontal orientation is used, maximizing the moment on the structure. Due to the

use of nonmetals in the construction, there would be a lack of stability as each link is being

supported by the previous one. This would further affect the accuracy and limit the accelerations

of the end effector. Lastly, it would be difficult to distance the actuators from the phantom itself,

making it difficult to avoid image artifacts.

By using a closed chain, the structure distributes the load across the several linkages for

enhanced stability. This also prevents mass and error from accumulating along each of the

linkages for improved accuracy and faster tool speeds/accelerations. Since all the linkages are

connected to the same end effector, this reduces the achievable workspace due to the

### 2.1.3 Transmission

After the delta configuration has been shown to be the best choice, an appropriate transmission

needs to be selected to convert the motion from the motors to the linear guides. The ideal

transmission is able to achieve high accuracies and speeds and be easy to set up in an MRI

environment.

2.1.3.1 Belt/Cables

Belts and cables are typically used in high-speed applications due to their lightweight and

smooth-running characteristics. Unlike gear trains, both belts and cables are easy to span

longer distances which can be helpful in separating the motors from the MRI. They don’t have to

be routed in a specific direction if more than one belt is being used, allowing for an extra degree

of control which is attractive. For example, if the robot is elevated, the belts or cables can still

route to the patient table so they are easy to mount. Challenges arise with set up and

maintenance since they must be tensioned properly for highest accuracy. Even with proper

tensioning, the elasticity of the belts or cables permits slack to affect the positioning accuracy.

Flat belts and cables are vulnerable to slip which can be avoided by using a timing belt where

the teeth would also help with changing directions.

2.1.3.2 Hydraulics/Pneumatics

Fluid can be forced through tubing to take advantage of Pascal’s Law to produce high force in

the output piston. Pneumatics uses pressurized air to accomplish this which is desirable

because it causes a minimal hazard in the case of a leak and requires lower maintenance

without the need for a reservoir. By using air, high speeds and accelerations can be achieved

due to the much lower mass and friction faced by the system. In contrast, hydraulics use liquids

as the fluid which changes many of the system’s characteristics. Hydraulics can produce much

stronger force outputs since they are far less compressible, although it is difficult to achieve

higher speeds and accelerations due to the increased mass and viscosity of the fluid. Both

options are as MRI friendly as it gets: they have an easy set up and the tubing can be run

through the waveguide with all electronics kept in the control room. Sadly, it is very difficult to

achieve a high positioning accuracy with them. Moreover, the pressures required to drive the

fluid through tubing at high speeds over long lengths is not practical according to the Hagen-

### 2.1.4 Actuator Selection

There are two classes of motors based on current type: AC and DC motors. AC motors are

generally used for continuous use applications due to their higher efficiency but suffer from

lower start up torque. Due to the use of sinusoidal currents, it would be expected to introduce

less noise in an MR environment since there are no sharp corners as there are in DC currents.

In contrast, DC motors have better position control and start/stop conditions. Since these are

essential to the project’s success, DC motors were selected.

Many types of DC motors exist: brushed, servo and stepper. Although they all use square

pulses to operate, several studies have shown to implement DC motors in an MR environment

[60], [61]. Brushed motors can be thought of as a bridge between AC and DC motors. They are

used for continuous high-speed RPM and are controlled by pulse width modulation. Servo

motors are known for high torque, speed and accuracy which is achieved through a closed loop

(servo) control system. They can further adjust their power according to a dynamic load,

however, DC servos are only capable of rotating <180°, due to the use of potentiometers. AC

servos work around this but are far more costly and complex to implement with performance

dropping largely around 300 hundred RPM. These servo control loops also introduce delays into

the system as it oscillates around the target value. Stepper motors move in discrete steps,

something which is unique compared to other motors. This ensures accuracy at a mechanical

level and helps with holding torque, or short movements. A trade off is made for lower efficiency

from high vibration and resonance. Although steppers tend to lose torque around 1000 RPM,

cost and control is far more manageable.

A special type of AC motor has been designed specifically for an MR environment. Piezoelectric

or ultrasonic motors are constructed from nonmagnetic materials, allowing them to be placed

anywhere in the MR scanner. However, they typically still introduce noise into images when they

are operating depending on how far from the region of interest they are. This is because they

use frequencies between 20 kHz and 10 MHz to create a controllable vibration, causing the

rotor to turn. Heat dissipation is a challenge with these motors because the mechanical

vibrations turn the rotor through friction between the surfaces. Similar to servo motors, a closed

### 2.1.6 Material Selection

It is imperative to choose the best suited materials to construct the parts in order to maximize

the product’s effectiveness. This complex selection process considers a number of factors and

trade offs depending on the application of the design. For the MR compatible robot, there are

several properties that need to be contemplated:

- Elastic modulus: high stiffness is required to achieve high positioning accuracy

- Electrical conductivity: low conductivity will avoid eddy currents

- Chemical stability:  materials should be inert and non reactive to the amniotic fluid

- Friction: low friction coefficients are ideal for parts experiencing wear through motion

- Hardness: increases wear resistance and longevity

- Manufacturability: parts are ideally easy to make from standard processes

- MR compatibility: minimal interaction with magnetic fields as discussed in section

1.5.2.3.

- Tensile strength: high strength prevents plastic deformation under loading

- Water absorption: low water absorption preserves the part shape and integrity

As per 1.5.2.3, the MR environment prohibits the use of metals in the robot which is not ideal

because plastics have far weaker mechanical properties than metals. This does however allow

3D printing processes to be taken advantage of to produce custom made parts given the low

The relay isolates the power to the drivers from the power applied to the board to prevent

### 2.4.1 Position Planning UI

Another MATLAB application was developed to assist with the position planning of the robot.

While path planning generally consists of position, speed and acceleration relations between the

end effector and active joints, this app is only capable of having the end effector reach targets

and not provide an accurate model of the path taken to reach these targets. With six pose

parameters to define for each point in time, there is a lot of information that needs to be inputted

and processed to create a motion profile. This information was broken down into several

components as shown in Figure 2.27 and Figure 2.28. A motion profile is defined by a routine; a

full path to travel. The routine consists of one or more splices, each defining an end target and a

base function to get there for each of the pose parameters (Pxyz and Rxyz). While each routine

has a unique sampling frequency, each splice has a duration which defines the speed. A

sampling frequency is only required when a sine function is used in one or more of the pose

parameters in any of the splices. It discretizes the curve into nodes for the robot to move to and

prevents the need to interpolate a linear function.

To begin coding, a library was selected to help easily program the steppers. There are three

## 4 Discussion

### 4.1 Comparative Analysis

There are four MRI compatible 6 DOF parallel robots that have been developed but not for

phantom applications. A summary of each of these designs alongside the design characteristics

of the robot developed in this work are presented in Table 4.1 below.

*Table 4.1) Comparison of the developed robot to 3 other MRI compatible 6 DOF parallel robots*

Each of the three other robots have been targeted towards procedures requiring the

manipulation of a needle with roughly half the load which is predominantly experienced in a

single direction. Additionally, reaching high speeds is not a priority. These differences in design

criteria allow for alternative actuation methods such as DEAs and pneumatics to be used. Due

to the use of a needle, a small amount of volume is taken at the end effector, permitting the

robot itself to be larger and, therefore, reach larger workspaces, especially for the Pneumatic

SG. The accuracies among each of the different designs are within 1 mm from each other

(disregarding the slider crank mechanism which only evaluated the accuracy of the actuators).


<!-- Page 90 -->


77

Only the pneumatic SG design quantified its imaging impacts and was able to achieve low SNR

degradations.

### 4.2 Limitations

The objectives of this thesis were to (1) design and build a six degrees of freedom (DOF) robot,

(2) assess the MR compatibility of the robot, and (3) evaluate the robot’s pose accuracy. To

measure the pose accuracy, a spherical phantom with a copper sulfate solution was used.

However, it inaccurately represents the target shape and material of the fetal phantom. Upon

synthesizing a fetal phantom, the impact of the robot on the imaging quality should be re-

evaluated for more contextual results since the amount of signal generated from the phantom

may be different. Additionally, the SNR measurement is subjective given that it is system

dependent due to the differences in operating principles for each MRI OEM as well as due to

natural drift in the magnetic fields over time.

Finally, the motion accuracy of the robot can be substantially improved by deriving the Jacobian.

This task will also permit computing the speed and acceleration at each point for complete path

planning which is required for accurate motion profiles. However, this was beyond the scope of

the current thesis but will be done in future iterations of the product.

### 4.3 Future work

Product development follows an endless cycle to allow for continuous improvement, hence,

despite everything completed to date, there are always aspects to build upon. Some of the most

urgent ones are listed here.

### 4.3.1 Robot Modifications

Carriage Joints

Upon reaching near straight angles along the vertical axis, the clevis locks up at its base

causing a fracture in the stem or pin mount (provide picture). Instead of having the 3D printed

disc at the base of the clevis, it can be replaced with the stem of the clevis in a bearing. This

reduces the friction from the large surface area of the disc and should prevent or at least reduce

the seizing of the joint.


<!-- Page 91 -->


78

Limit Switch Mounts

Currently triangular shaped plates are being used to mount the limit switches to the central hub

of the linear guides. This requires the limit switches to be placed on top of the hub with

extensions added to the levers so they are contacted by the carriages. The number of parts can

be reduced while increasing stability and accuracy through incorporating the limit switches

directly into the central hub at the level of the carriages.

Bearing Covers

Particularly at the U joints, the bearings occasionally pull out because of the angled forces and

vibrations exerted on them. Covers can be placed on the open faces of the housing to prevent

bearings from pulling out.

Motor structure

After the upgrades performed at the MRI site at the Hospital for Sick Children, the table end was

changed, no longer fitting the motor stand properly. The structure supporting the motors needs

to be redesigned to fit on the new table. Ideally, this stand would also be adjustable to fit other

patient tables. Aluminum T slotted bars may be a great way to provide strength and flexibility.

3D Printed Material

For this first iteration of the robot, all resin parts were printed in the standard resin. This was a

great way to test the functionality of the mechanisms but other materials are better suited for

some parts. Namely, the lead screws should be printed in the durable resin as it is the most

lubricous to reduce friction and wear. The rigid resin can also be used for some parts requiring

strength and rigidity with a smooth surface finish such as the platform.

Vibration Dampening

The steppers generate significant vibrations operating in full step mode. It would be desirable to

reduce the vibrations before they are carried through the electronics and driving shafts.

Vibration dampening sheets may be beneficial to use between the motors and the panel, or

vibration dampening shaft couplers.

### 4.3.2 PCB Modifications

Pin/Trace Optimization

Several modifications can be made to the pin assignment of the shield as touched on in PCB

and Accessories. Pin 1 can be routed to 16 instead. On the relay, the trace can be connected to

the NO pin instead of the NC pin to prevent the need for the bridge. Overall, the number of pins

used can be reduced by removing the redundancy that was included for testing purposes,

namely, the negative voltage encoder pins and the 5V for the limit switches.

A trace could be added to the drivers for active gain control. This will allow for the drawn current

to be controlled to match the torque required. By regulating the current drawn, heat dissipation

can be improved.

Although it hasn’t been tested, the implementation of pull up resistors on the breakout board for

the encoders and limit switches may help with the response of the components.

Connectors

Since the redundant pins are being removed, an entire DB9 connector is not needed, and since

they are stacked on the board, an entire stack can be removed with an existing NC. The area of

the board can be reduced and the remaining connections condensed since the motor

connectors all have a NC pin.

Soldering the 18 AWG wires to the solder cups of the DB9 connectors to make the motor cables

was largely undesirable. It was difficult to work with the apparatus and the connections often

broke, even after adding the back shells. Purchasing DB9 cables of appropriate gauge or using

a different cable with adapters is highly recommended.

The limit switches should use a connector instead of a terminal block on the breakout board.

The many thin wires are very tedious to work with and the terminal blocks take up a lot of space.

It would also simplify the breakout board housing if the GX16 aviation connectors could be

installed directly onto the board; at the time, no board mounted components could be found. It

might even be easier to cut out mounting holes in the board and solder wires into holes adjacent

to the connector.

Solder Mask

The top overlay can be improved by making things more clearly labeled to help with debugging

and setting up. It was especially a bit more challenging on the breakout board since the

connectors were not in order to help with proximity and routing traces. The +/- on the power

terminal block needs to be reversed.

Motor Power Traces

As mentioned in section 6.2) PCB, the motor power traces were undersized intentionally as a

quick fix. To prevent the need for soldering external wires, there are a couple of different options

that may be more reliable and user friendly. Bus bars could be used to route the power as one

option. Alternatively, power planes could be used on a 4-layer PCB, although it may even be

possible to have local power planes on a 2-layer PCB if carefully designed. This means only the

regions with the circuit protection components and those extending to the drivers would use

power planes, but the rest of the PCB would not. Lastly, using a motor with a reduced current

rating is also an option. It would not be ideal to increase the copper thickness since only a small

portion of the board would actually require such large thicknesses, the signal traces typically

use very small currents.

Forced Airflow

Mounting a fan over the drivers will help cool them to run at the rated 2A for long periods of

time. It is possible that the drivers overheated during testing after ~15 min of continuous

operation. It would be desirable to have them operate up to an hour as MRI scan sessions for

research purposes are usually a minimum of an hour long.

### 4.3.3 Software Improvements

User Interface

The Arduino and Processing scripts have provided a good foundation to allow users to visualize

key information and are more user friendly than the Arduino scripts alone. Many additional

features could be implemented in the future to enhance the user experience. In the case of

many experiments, it could be beneficial to home the robot and upload new paths without

exiting the application to save time. It would also be beneficial to have some sort of visual

feedback of the robot’s position as it executes the path such as a wire frame of the robot or a

simple coordinate system showing the pose of the end effector. For motion simulations, ROS

may be able to address our needs. It was recommended that to interface with the MRI, a trigger

line could be implemented for gated imaging procedures, widely expanding the possible modes

of experimentation with the phantom.

Script Optimization

There are some features that were challenging to add and therefore, never fully implemented.

Using micro stepping for accelerating the transmissions and then transitioning to full steps

allows for much smoother movement at low speeds, higher stopping accuracy, and still permits

higher speeds to be achieved. Using the SpeedyStepper and FlexyStepper libraries, it was

found that changing the steps per millimeter during movements caused a strange interaction

between motor speed being scaled and requiring acceleration to reach the newly scaled speed.

Changing the speed before the step size or vice versa was found to have the same result.

Sinusoidal motion exported from Signal Lab was found to be very inconsistent and create a

jittery motion. Root causes for this are unknown, although it is suspected that it may involve the

few steps that are required to reach the close together discrete points with a required

acceleration to reach the target speed.

### 4.3.4 Respiratory and Cardiac Motion

To incorporate respiratory motion in the phantom, a tube can be inserted into the chest cavity of

the fetus to pump air resulting in expansion of the chest. This tube must be flexible and be

sufficient length to allow the gross body movement. It should also be as thin as possible to avoid

introducing an image artifact by displacing amniotic fluid. While the respiratory motion can be

driven by a ventilator, the same concepts can be implemented for cardiac motion but driven by a

pump.

## 5 Conclusions

Birth defects are a serious problem that can impair the life of newborns and families. Fetal

diagnostic imaging has been slow to develop new technologies for overcoming motion related

challenges. The development of anthropomorphic motion phantoms shows great promise for

accelerating data acquisition, reducing research costs, and results in image processing

algorithms with improved reliability and more robust sequences. Unfortunately, few phantoms

incorporate sources of motion currently. Through this project, a research tool was developed to

house the peripheral phantoms of the gravid abdomen with a motion device to implement

physiological motion sources in the fetal phantom. This also entailed the development of a

shield for the Arduino, a breakout board, and three software components to assist the user in

position planning and robot control. The robot’s positioning accuracy was assessed to be ±2.1

mm, which is a reasonable starting point based on our literature review and comparative

analysis with other existing mechanisms. Nonetheless, the robot dynamics can be improved

upon in future works by deriving and utilizing the Jacobian. This robotic mechanism which is

targeted as a research tool has been shown to only degrade image SNR by less than 2% at 3T

and a maximum B0 variation of 1 ppm, supporting its MR compatibility and minimal EMI.

Prospective efforts will push towards achieving higher accuracies, additional motion sources,

and enhanced user experiences to achieve the highest standard and most comprehensive MRI

phantoms of the gravid abdomen.
